summary.title: ArtisanMarket API Threat Model
summary.description: Plan-stage threat model (Section 4.3.1) for the ArtisanMarket API (Node.js 20, Express 4, ES modules; MongoDB via Mongoose; optional Redis; Socket.IO; Stripe, Plaid and ImageKit; deployed as a non-root container on Kubernetes). Covers authentication, products and vendors, orders and checkout, balances, bank account linking and media upload. The API is the trust boundary: every authorisation decision is made here, and nothing the SPA sends is trusted.

data.name: Container runtime (Kubernetes)
data.description: API container built from the multi-stage Dockerfile and deployed with the k8s/ manifests under the restricted Pod Security Standard.

threats.title: Vulnerable container base image
threats.description: Operating-system packages or the Node runtime in the base image could carry known CVEs.
threats.mitigation: Trivy image scan at Build against the image built from the multi-stage Dockerfile (node:20-alpine). The first scan found 26 findings (1 CRITICAL): 22 came from npm's bundled dependency tree and were removed by deleting npm from the runtime stage, where it is never invoked; the rest were openssl libcrypto3/libssl3, upgraded explicitly. The container runs as non-root UID 10001. Clean at CRITICAL/HIGH and re-verified daily by the scheduled run. SEED-IMAGE-01 shows the gate firing.

data.name: SPA / browser client
data.description: Shoppers, vendors and administrators, via the ArtisanMarket React SPA in a browser. Untrusted: every request it sends is attacker-controllable.

data.name: Express API
data.description: Node.js 20 / Express 4 application: routes/, middleware/, models/. Authorises every privileged action and serves REST and Socket.IO.

data.name: Environment secrets
data.description: JWT_SECRET, BANK_ENCRYPTION_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET, PLAID_*, IMAGEKIT_*. Supplied by the deployment environment; never committed.

threats.title: Hard-coded credential fallbacks
threats.description: Eleven call sites across six files fell back to a literal when a credential variable was unset. With JWT_SECRET unset, admin and vendor tokens were verified against the public constant 'fallback-secret', so sessions were forgeable. Stripe and Plaid clients fell back to placeholder credentials.
threats.mitigation: Remediated. config/secrets.js getJwtSecret() throws when the secret is absent, and server.js calls assertRequiredSecrets(['JWT_SECRET']), so the process refuses to start without it. Admin and vendor token verification use getJwtSecret(); the auth routes and auth middleware read JWT_SECRET directly, which is safe only because startup has already asserted it. routes/mockApi.js, which held three of the sites, has been deleted. Stripe and Plaid clients are constructed only when their credentials exist. The Code-stage ESLint rule blocks the process.env.<SECRET> || '<literal>' pattern, and SEED-SAST-01 shows it firing.

data.name: Application logs
data.description: Request, error and health-monitor logs written to stdout.

threats.title: Credentials and payment data in logs, and forged log lines
threats.description: Error logging that echoes request headers or bodies records tokens, passwords and card or account numbers. Unsanitised input in a log line can forge entries and hide real activity (jssecurity:S5145).
threats.mitigation: middleware/errorHandler.js redacts authorisation, cookie, API-key, signature and token headers, and body fields matching password, token, secret, card, account, CVV, PIN and similar markers. Its tests caught a real bug: camelCase field names such as cardNumber bypassed the marker list, so card numbers were still being logged before the fix. utils/sanitize.js forLog strips control characters and caps length at each logging site in the request path and in the health monitor.

data.name: MongoDB
data.description: Users, products, orders, balances and encrypted bank account details, via Mongoose.

threats.title: Bank account details encrypted without integrity
threats.description: Bank account details are encrypted at rest with AES-256-CBC (utils/encryption.js). CBC gives confidentiality but no authentication: anyone with write access to the database can alter stored ciphertext undetected, and observable decryption failures can act as a padding oracle (SonarQube javascript:S5542, CRITICAL).
threats.mitigation: Risk accepted for this iteration. The correct algorithm, AES-256-GCM, changes the stored format, so every existing record must be decrypted under CBC and re-encrypted under GCM in a migration; done wrongly, it leaves financial data permanently unreadable. Compensating controls: the key is never committed (Gitleaks), must be exactly 64 hex characters, and the process refuses to start without it. Tracked in docs/evidence/finding-ledger.md. Remediation path: AES-256-GCM with a re-encryption migration.

data.name: packages

threats.title: Vulnerable or compromised dependency
threats.description: A direct or transitive package could ship a known vulnerability or malicious code. Build tooling runs in CI with repository access even though it never ships in the image.
threats.mitigation: Two blocking SCA gates over the full tree, devDependencies included: npm audit on every branch through scripts/audit-gate.js, which accepts a named advisory only with a reason and a review date (.audit-allowlist.json) and judges each advisory on its own severity; and a Trivy dependency scan at Build. Snyk is wired in as optional and is not configured. The Monitor stage re-runs both daily. Between 2026-10-05 and 2026-10-07 this caught critical advisories in proxy-addr (runtime) and shell-quote (dev tooling), both fixed, and accepted braces (no fix exists; dev-only) until 2026-12-05. cloudinary and nodemailer were removed as unused.

data.name: image + manifests
data.description: Container image and Kubernetes manifests.

threats.title: Misconfigured deployment manifests
threats.description: Kubernetes manifests could run containers as root, omit resource limits or leave network paths open.
threats.mitigation: Checkov at Build against k8s/. The namespace enforces the restricted Pod Security Standard, so drift is rejected at admission rather than merely reported, and a NetworkPolicy restricts traffic; SEED-IAC-01 (NetworkPolicy deleted) shows Checkov's graph check CKV2_K8S_6 firing. Two documented in-band exceptions: CKV_K8S_43, because the image digest is substituted at deploy, and CKV_K8S_35, a real gap accepted rather than dismissed: secrets reach the app as environment variables, tracked for migration to file-mounted secrets.

data.name: API requests (Bearer JWT)
data.description: Authenticated REST and Socket.IO requests carrying query and body values.

threats.title: NoSQL operator injection through request values
threats.description: Express parses ?status[$ne]=x into an object. Assigned straight into a Mongoose filter it injects query operators ($ne, $gt, $regex, $where) and changes what the query matches; on a login route that is an authentication bypass. A caller-supplied pattern passed to new RegExp() was also a ReDoS vector.
threats.mitigation: utils/sanitize.js coerces request values before they reach a filter: asString rejects objects, asEnum restricts values to allow-lists, and asSafeSearchRegex escapes metacharacters and caps the term at 100 characters. Used across eight route files alongside express-validator. Integration tests assert that an operator object can neither authenticate nor alter a query. SonarQube still reports 8 jssecurity:S5147 findings on guarded call sites because its taint analysis does not follow a custom sanitiser; these are documented false positives (docs/evidence/quality-gate.md).

data.name: login / register
data.description: Credential submission to /api/auth.

threats.title: Credential stuffing and brute force on login
threats.description: Automated password guessing or credential stuffing against /api/auth/login and /api/auth/register.
threats.mitigation: express-rate-limit on /api/ caps each IP at 100 requests per 15 minutes (RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_MS, RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS). Residual risk: the limit is per IP and shared by every endpoint, so a distributed attack is not slowed and authentication has no stricter limit of its own. Recommended next step: a dedicated limiter on /api/auth.

data.name: image upload (multipart)
data.description: Product image upload to /api/upload.

threats.title: Upload volume exhausting memory or storage
threats.description: Uploads are buffered in memory (multer memoryStorage) and forwarded to ImageKit. Large or numerous uploads could exhaust the heap or storage, and unrestricted types could serve hostile files.
threats.mitigation: In place, per request: a MIME allow-list (JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF; SVG rejected), at most 4 files of 5 MB each (20 MB buffered), and limits on fields and parts, covered by tests/uploadFilter.test.js. Not addressed: there is no per-user quota, so total volume across requests is bounded only by the global per-IP rate limit. The MIME type is caller-supplied, so the allow-list bounds the obvious cases rather than proving content.

data.name: products, stores, reviews
data.description: Vendor- and user-supplied content returned for rendering, with response headers.

threats.title: Stored script in vendor- and user-supplied text
threats.description: Product descriptions, store names and review comments are stored and returned to the SPA verbatim. A render path that treated them as HTML would execute them as script for later visitors (stored XSS).
threats.mitigation: Mitigated at the render boundary, not in the API. The SPA renders through React's default escaping, and its Code-stage ESLint and SonarQube rules block dangerouslySetInnerHTML and innerHTML (client threat T2). The API does not sanitise or encode text on write, so any consumer other than the React SPA must escape on output. There is currently no review-submission endpoint; reviews are embedded in product documents.

threats.title: Missing security headers and technology disclosure
threats.description: Without security response headers, responses are easier to frame, sniff or execute in a browser, and the X-Powered-By header discloses the framework.
threats.mitigation: helmet is applied in server.js with a strict Content-Security-Policy for a JSON API (default-src 'none', frame-ancestors 'none', base-uri 'none', form-action 'none'); crossOriginEmbedderPolicy is disabled. CORS is restricted to an origin allow-list (CLIENT_URL, CORS_ORIGINS). The Staging OWASP ZAP baseline runs against the live API; SEED-DAST-01 (helmet removed) shows it detecting the change through the X-Powered-By disclosure rule.

data.name: webhook events
data.description: Stripe event notifications to /api/payments/webhook.

threats.title: Forged payment webhook
threats.description: Stripe webhooks change order and balance state. A forged request could mark an order paid.
threats.mitigation: routes/paymentRoutes.js verifies every event with stripe.webhooks.constructEvent and STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET over a raw body, preserved by express.raw ahead of JSON parsing. An invalid signature, or a missing secret, returns 400 before any state changes, so the handler fails closed.
